title: Design a News Feed
subtitle: Balance feed write amplification, read-time merging, ranking, and pagination
objectives: Frame the feed as a read-heavy problem and estimate what that costs
Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read, and locate where each one breaks
Explain the celebrity problem and why the real answer is a hybrid
Handle ranking, pagination, and consistency in a feed people scroll

exercises.title: A news feed is a personalized, usually read-heavy view
exercises.body: A feed selects posts from accounts one user follows, so its result differs by user. The service can assemble that view on each read or materialize a per-user candidate list as posts arrive. Materialization shifts repeated read work into writes and storage.
exercises.note: Assembling on demand makes read cost grow with follow count; maintaining views shifts that cost to writes and consumes per-user storage.

exercises.prompt: A celebrity with 15 million followers publishes a post. Stop copying it into every follower inbox; merge it during feed reads instead.
exercises.actionLabel: Switch the celebrity to fan-out on read
exercises.afterStatus: ONE CELEBRITY POST · 1 post write; readers merge the celebrity stream
exercises.why: Fan-out on read avoids millions of writes for a celebrity post by merging that author's stream when followers read. Read work increases, so production feeds commonly push normal accounts and pull high-fan-out accounts.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A celebrity with 15 million followers publishes a post. Stop copying it into every follower inbox; merge it during feed reads instead. Place Feed reader, Feed response. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Celebrity posts → Feed reader; User timeline → Feed reader; Feed reader → Feed response. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Fan-out on read avoids millions of writes for a celebrity post by merging that author's stream when followers read. Read work increases, so production feeds commonly push normal accounts and pull high-fan-out accounts.

exercises.prompt: 'Design a news feed.' What's the defining characteristic of this workload?
choices: It's brutally read-heavy and personalized: everyone's feed is different, and people refresh far more than they post
exercises.why: Feed reads greatly outnumber posts, and each result depends on the reader's follow graph and ranking context. The design therefore needs a low-cost personalized read path, typically backed by per-user materialization, efficient candidate retrieval, or both.

exercises.prompt: 300 million daily users opening the feed 10 times each creates 3 billion reads/day, about 34,700 reads/sec on average before peaks. What should this drive in the design?
choices: Build each personalized feed with a large join and sort on every read
Make the common feed read close to a bounded lookup over prepared candidates
Store every user's complete feed on the phone only
Send every post synchronously to every follower before acknowledging it
exercises.why: At roughly 34,700 average reads/sec, expensive per-read joins and sorts multiply into sustained database and compute load, with higher demand at peaks. Preparing a bounded candidate list makes the common read a predictable lookup plus limited hydration or ranking work.

exercises.prompt: The obvious approach: when a user opens the feed, query for all posts by everyone they follow, sorted by time. Why won't that survive?
choices: You'd run a huge multi-follow query, sort it, and paginate it — tens of thousands of times a second, and the cost scales with how many people each user follows
exercises.why: For each refresh, the query gathers posts from hundreds of followed accounts and sorts the combined result. Repeating that fan-in at tens of thousands of reads per second creates high read amplification even with useful indexes, so the system should bound or precompute more of the work.

exercises.prompt: Building each feed at read time is called fan-out on ______.
exercises.why: Fan-out on read fetches and merges posts from all followed accounts when the feed request arrives. Its cost grows with the number of followed accounts and directly adds to user-visible latency.

exercises.prompt: Given the roughly 100:1 read:write ratio, where can you move repeated feed-assembly work?
choices: Put the work where the traffic isn't — do it at write time, so a read becomes one cheap lookup
exercises.why: When reads substantially outnumber posts, precomputing follower feed entries once at post time can avoid repeating the same merge work on many reads. This shifts cost to writes and storage in exchange for a cheaper, more predictable read path.

exercises.prompt: So what does 'fan-out on write' actually do?
choices: It writes the post to a queue
When you post, it immediately inserts that post's id into the precomputed feed list of every one of your followers
It replicates the post to every server
exercises.why: Fan-out on write appends a new post ID to each follower's materialized feed when the post is created. A later feed request reads one bounded, precomputed list, so its work depends primarily on the requested page size and hydration cost.

exercises.title: Fan-out on write materializes follower feeds asynchronously
exercises.body: The publish transaction stores one canonical post and a durable outbox record for fan-out. A dispatcher enqueues that record; workers append the post id to follower feed lists. Feed reads fetch a bounded list of ids and hydrate the posts.
exercises.note: The outbox closes the crash gap between storing the post and publishing work. One post still causes O(F) list writes for F followers.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when a user with 200 followers posts, using fan-out on write.
steps: One transaction stores the post and a durable fan-out outbox record
Server responds — the post and its pending distribution are durable
An outbox dispatcher publishes the fan-out job to the queue
A worker looks up the author's 200 followers
The post id is appended to each of those 200 feed lists
exercises.why: Storing the post and outbox record in one transaction ensures that an acknowledged post cannot lose its distribution work if the server crashes. A dispatcher can retry publishing the durable outbox record, and idempotent workers can retry appends; the follower-count-dependent writes remain off the request latency path.

exercises.prompt: Why store the post ONCE and push only its id into follower feeds, rather than copying the post itself?
choices: Copying the post 200 times means 200 places to update when it's edited or deleted — the id keeps one source of truth and makes the feed a list of pointers
exercises.why: The post store remains the source of truth, while feed lists contain rebuildable post IDs. Copying the full body into each list would reduce hydration reads but would require updating or deleting every copy when the post changes or is removed.

exercises.prompt: A user with 200 million followers posts. What does fan-out on write do?
choices: Attempts 200 million list writes for one post — a single action becomes hours of work and a massive write storm
Fans out only to active followers
exercises.why: Fan-out-on-write cost grows linearly with follower count. A post to 200 million followers creates 200 million list updates, producing a write storm and queue backlog from one event, so this author class needs a different delivery path.

exercises.prompt: Beyond the write storm, what's the second-order damage from a celebrity fan-out?
choices: It's not instant — followers at the end of the queue see the post minutes after followers at the front, so the feed becomes visibly unfair
The database runs out of space
exercises.why: Workers update follower lists over time, so a large fan-out makes visibility depend on queue position. During a live event, early followers may see the post minutes before later followers, creating user-visible propagation skew in addition to backend load.

exercises.prompt: What does fan-out on write cost you? Select all.
choices: Write amplification proportional to follower count
Storage for every user's materialized feed list
Wasted work for inactive users who never read their feed
exercises.why: Fan-out on write performs one materialized-feed update per recipient, consumes storage for those lists, and may write entries for inactive users who never read them. This write and storage cost precomputes feed membership, giving subsequent reads a bounded retrieval path with less fan-in and sorting.

exercises.prompt: How do you stop fanning out to users who never read their feed?
choices: Only fan out to recently-active users, and build the feed on demand for anyone who returns after a long absence
exercises.why: Suppressing fan-out for inactive accounts avoids writes and storage for feeds unlikely to be read. When such a user returns, the system can rebuild recent candidates with a one-time fan-out-on-read query, trading occasional return latency for lower steady write amplification.

exercises.title: A hybrid feed selects fan-out strategy by author fan-out cost
exercises.body: Posts from ordinary accounts are pushed into follower feed lists at write time. Posts from high-follower accounts remain in the post store. A feed read fetches its materialized list, queries recent posts from followed high-follower accounts, merges the candidates, and ranks them.
exercises.note: The threshold is an operational parameter derived from follower distribution, queue capacity, acceptable propagation delay, and read budget.

exercises.prompt: Fan-out-on-write works for ordinary authors, but one celebrity with 30 million followers creates a huge write burst. Change only the celebrity path.
exercises.afterStatus: CELEBRITY POST · 1 post write · merged during reads
exercises.result: The exceptional fan-out no longer blocks the publishing path
exercises.why: A hybrid feed pushes ordinary posts into follower inboxes and pulls high-fan-out authors during reads. The threshold should follow measured write amplification and read cost; celebrity status itself is only a proxy.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: Fan-out-on-write works for ordinary authors, but one celebrity with 30 million followers creates a huge write burst. Change only the celebrity path. Place Author posts, Feed merge, Follower feed. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Celebrity post → Author posts; Author posts → Feed merge; Feed merge → Follower feed. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A hybrid feed pushes ordinary posts into follower inboxes and pulls high-fan-out authors during reads. The threshold should follow measured write amplification and read cost; celebrity status itself is only a proxy.

exercises.prompt: Build the hybrid feed read: combine pushed ordinary posts with pulled celebrity posts before returning a page.
exercises.why: The feed service reads the precomputed list for ordinary authors, pulls recent posts only from followed high-follower authors, then merges and ranks both candidate sets. Pushing celebrity posts would create a write storm, while pulling every followed author's posts would restore the unbounded read-time fan-in the materialized list avoids.

exercises.prompt: Order how a hybrid feed read assembles.
steps: Fetch the user's precomputed feed list
Fetch recent posts from the few celebrities they follow
exercises.why: The read combines one prepared candidate list with a query over the limited set of high-follower authors the user follows, then ranks the merged candidates. Lowering the exclusion threshold increases read-time work; raising it increases write fan-out and queue pressure.

exercises.prompt: Where do you set the celebrity threshold — the follower count above which you stop fanning out?
choices: Wherever the fan-out cost stops being worth it, judged from your own distribution — it's an operational number you tune, not a constant
It should be dynamic per post
exercises.why: The threshold should be selected from measured follower distributions, fan-out throughput, queue-delay targets, and acceptable read-time merge cost. It controls a continuous tradeoff: more authors above the threshold reduce write amplification while increasing live query work.

exercises.prompt: Where should each user's precomputed feed list actually live?
choices: In a fast store like Redis, capped at a few hundred entries — it's derived data, rebuildable from posts and follows, so it doesn't need the durability of the source of truth
exercises.why: A feed list is derived from durable posts and follows, so it can use a fast store and be rebuilt after loss. Capping the list bounds per-user memory and write work while retaining the recent candidate window the product actually serves.

exercises.prompt: Your feed lists are in Redis. Redis restarts and loses everything. How bad?
choices: Recoverable but painful: feeds rebuild from posts and follows, so nothing is truly lost — but every read now falls through to expensive rebuilds at once
exercises.why: Losing materialized feed lists does not destroy authoritative posts or follow relationships, so they can be rebuilt. During recovery, concurrent reads can trigger many identical reconstruction queries, so the system needs staged warming, request coalescing, or rate-limited rebuilds to protect the source stores.

exercises.prompt: A user follows someone new. What has to happen to their feed?
choices: Nothing — new posts will fan out to them
New posts arrive naturally, but the new followee's EXISTING posts aren't in the list — so you either backfill them or accept the feed only fills in going forward
The whole feed must be rebuilt
exercises.why: Fan-out on write delivers only posts created after the follow relationship exists. Showing older posts requires a backfill that inserts recent post IDs from the new account; products may limit that work or allow the feed to fill forward based on latency and experience requirements.

exercises.title: Fan-out produces candidates; read-time ranking produces order
exercises.body: A materialized feed stores candidate post ids. At read time, a ranker scores those candidates using post features, reader features, and current context, then returns the highest-scoring page. Context-dependent relevance cannot be finalized when the author publishes.
exercises.note: Cap the candidate set before scoring; ranker latency and compute cost grow with the number and complexity of candidates evaluated per read.

exercises.prompt: Your feed is ranked by relevance, not time. What does that break about fan-out on write?
choices: The precomputed list was ordered at write time, but relevance depends on the reader and the moment — so you can no longer bake the final order in advance
exercises.why: Fan-out can materialize a bounded set of eligible post IDs, but relevance may depend on current reader context and model features that change after posting. Ranking those prepared candidates at read time preserves personalization while avoiding a scan over the full post corpus.

exercises.prompt: Your feed uses ?offset=40&limit=20 for the third page. New posts arrive while the user scrolls. What do they see?
choices: Duplicates: new posts shifted everything down, so items they already saw are pushed into the next page
exercises.why: Offset pagination counts positions from a list boundary that changes whenever a new post is inserted at the top. Those insertions shift later offsets, causing duplicate or skipped items between requests.

exercises.prompt: A relevance-ranked feed can rescore while the user scrolls. How should pagination handle that?
choices: Use an offset into the latest ranking
Use a cursor with the last ordering key and tie-breaker plus a ranking snapshot/version, or explicitly accept duplicates and skips from reranking
exercises.why: A timestamp or score plus a unique post ID gives a deterministic position only while the ordering remains stable. Because relevance scores can change between requests, the cursor also needs a ranking snapshot or version to reproduce that order; without one, the product must accept pagination drift such as duplicates or skipped posts.

exercises.prompt: Which parts of a feed can be eventually consistent? Select all.
choices: A followee's post appearing in your feed a few seconds late
The like count on a post
Your own post appearing in your own profile immediately after posting
A blocked user's posts continuing to appear
exercises.why: Friend-post propagation and aggregate like counts can tolerate bounded staleness because small delays or count errors do not violate the core action. A user's own post needs read-your-writes behavior, and a block must affect authorization immediately because exposing blocked content is a safety and privacy failure.

exercises.prompt: A user deletes a post that's already been fanned out to 200,000 feed lists. Slide toward your approach.
exercises.leftLabel: Purge it from all 200,000 lists now
exercises.rightLabel: Leave the ids; filter deleted posts at read time
exercises.why: Because feed lists contain IDs, read-time hydration can omit an ID whose authoritative post has been deleted, avoiding synchronous edits to 200,000 lists. Safety or legal deletion requirements may additionally require eager invalidation and audited removal because a missed read-time filter could expose prohibited content.

exercises.prompt: Summarize the news feed design.
choices: Query posts from followees at read time, cached
Precompute feeds on write for ordinary users, query live for celebrities, merge and rank at read time — with cursor pagination and derived lists you can rebuild
A graph database traversal per read
exercises.why: The hybrid precomputes feed candidates for ordinary authors and queries high-follower authors at read time, controlling both read amplification and write storms. Derived bounded lists support recovery, read-time ranking applies current context, and cursor pagination remains stable as new posts enter the top of the feed.

exercises.title: The source post is authoritative; inbox entries are rebuildable candidate references
exercises.body: A post commit emits durable fan-out work. Ordinary authors push post IDs into bounded follower inboxes; high-fan-out authors are pulled during reads. The read service merges candidates, filters current visibility policy, hydrates authoritative posts, ranks, and returns a cursor-stable page.
exercises.note: An inbox entry grants no visibility. Deletes, blocks, and privacy changes must be checked against authoritative policy during hydration so stale derived IDs cannot expose content.

exercises.prompt: A private post was already copied into follower inboxes. The author blocks one follower, but that follower's next feed read still returns the post.
choices: Wait for every inbox copy to expire
Authorize each hydrated post against current relationship and post policy
choiceFeedback: Expiry creates an uncontrolled privacy window.
Read-time authorization prevents stale candidate references from becoming visible content.
Deleting unrelated candidates is unnecessary and still does not define future policy checks.
exercises.beforeStatus: STALE INBOX ID · blocked follower receives private post
exercises.afterStatus: CANDIDATE FOUND · current policy denies hydration
exercises.result: Derived feed state can lag without violating visibility
exercises.why: Fan-out materializes candidates under an earlier social graph. Because blocks and privacy are safety invariants, the read path must evaluate current policy before returning content rather than treating an inbox ID as authorization.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A private post was already copied into follower inboxes. The author blocks one follower, but that follower's next feed read still returns the post. Place Visibility policy, User response. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Feed inbox → Visibility policy; Visibility policy → User response. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Fan-out materializes candidates under an earlier social graph. Because blocks and privacy are safety invariants, the read path must evaluate current policy before returning content rather than treating an inbox ID as authorization.

exercises.prompt: Build the hybrid read path that combines precomputed ordinary-author posts with celebrity posts.
exercises.why: The hybrid bounds ordinary read work without paying celebrity fan-out. Both candidate sets meet before current-policy filtering, authoritative hydration, and ranking; cursor state then continues from the returned ordering boundary.

exercises.prompt: Which review findings are genuine design defects? Select all.
choices: Full post bodies are copied into every follower inbox
Celebrity fan-out shares the same queue and workers as ordinary posts
Offset pagination is used on a changing ranked list
Feed candidates are treated as permission to display a post
exercises.why: Copying bodies multiplies storage and update work, unisolated celebrity fan-out starves ordinary delivery, offsets drift as ranking changes, and candidate references can outlive the policy that originally admitted them. Each defect appears only when the complete write and read paths are considered together.

exercises.prompt: A project dashboard shows updates from followed repositories. One repository has ten million followers. Which delivery design avoids ten million synchronous writes on each update?
choices: Always fan out every update before acknowledging it
Pull or hybrid fan-out for the exceptional publisher
exercises.why: The celebrity repository makes fan-out-on-write proportional to ten million followers. A hybrid keeps ordinary publishers precomputed while pulling exceptional publishers during reads.
